column2: Such a one, endowed with such valour and qualities, with Krishna as his second, I choose for battle, protected by immeasurably valiant Keshava, the incomparable Narayana.

His qualities could not be told in ten thousand years even by all the worlds together—of the great-souled bearer of conch, discus and sword, Vishnu, Jishnu, Vasudeva's son; fear and dread arise in me at seeing the two Krishnas together on one chariot.
Both are brave, accomplished, firm in weapons, great chariot-warriors, endowed with strong frames; such are Phalguna and Vasudeva; who other than I, Shalya, would face them?
I shall fell these two in battle, or the two Krishnas will slay me today—" so saying, Karna, able to slay foes, roared in the battle like a cloud.

Welcomed by your son who came up, he met the Kuru heroes and said to Kripa, to Bhoja, to the two mighty-armed ones, to the king of Gandhara with his younger brothers, to Drona's son and his own younger brother, and to the foot-soldiers, elephant-men and others:
Hold back and attack Achyuta and Arjuna; quickly bring them to exhaustion on every side, so that, both much wounded by you, I may slay them easily today, kings of the earth.
Saying "So be it," those best of heroes quickly advanced on Arjuna, wishing to kill him; Arjuna swallowed them in battle as the great ocean with its much water swallows rivers.
He was not seen by the foes either aiming or loosing the best of arrows; torn by Dhananjaya's arrows, the slain men, horses and elephants fell.
The Kauravas could not look at him whose arrows were rays, whose Gandiva was a fair circle, whose splendour was like the sun at the end of an age, as people with diseased eyes cannot look at the sun.

Kripa rushed at him, loosing arrows, and so did Bhoja and your son himself; the Pandava, in haste, cut with arrows those best of arrows, swift and carefully aimed by the skilled ones eager to kill him, and pierced them in the chest with three each.
Arjuna, scorching his foes with the full circle of the bow Gandiva, shone with his arrow-rays fierce, like the sun between Shukra and pure Brihaspati, as the sun in its halo.
Then Drona's son pierced Dhananjaya with ten fine arrows and Achyuta with three; and he covered his four horses and the monkey with four and the best iron arrows.
Then Dhananjaya, with three arrows, struck off his charioteer's head, took his quivering bow, and felled from Drona's son's chariot his four horses with four and his banner with three.
Filled with fury, he took another bow with good fittings, adorned with thunderbolt and gold, with the sheen of the serpent Takshaka's coils, like a great serpent on a mountain.
Casting his own weapon on the ground and stringing his bow, the excellent bowstring-bearer, Drona's son pierced from close by the unconquered best of men on their chariot with the finest arrows.
Kripa and Bhoja and your son attacked like clouds on the dispeller of darkness; Partha cut Kripa's bow with its arrow, his horses, banner and charioteer with feathered arrows.
He cut your son's banner and bow as he roared, killed the fair horses of Kritavarman, and the valiant one then cut his banner.

He killed the steel-clad on horses and charioteers with their banners, the elephants, horses and chariots, in haste; then your great army was scattered and torn like a dam by water. Then Keshava in Arjuna's chariot made his foes circle to the left, as mothers do.
As Dhananjaya went swiftly, like Shatakratu who slew Vritra, other keen warriors followed again with raised banners and well-yoked chariots.
Then Shikhandin, Shaineya and the twins, great chariot-warriors, approached Dhananjaya's chariot, held back those foes and, tearing them with sharp arrows, roared very fiercely.
Then the Kuru heroes with the Srinjayas struck each other, enraged, with arrows of straight course and keen edge, as in the old days the asuras fought the best of the gods.
Eager for victory and keen to go to heaven, elephants, horses and chariots fell, scorcher of foes; they roared aloud and strongly pierced each other with well-loosed arrows, one by one.
When the great souls made a darkness of arrows in that great battle among the best of warriors, O king, the ten quarters and the sky and the sun's light were covered with darkness.
Having crushed the charioteer's son's army with arrows, O Bharata, Dhananjaya sent heroes to the world of mortals' death.
Then nets of arrows covering the sky, by portions, were seen, and others slaying your army.
Filling with arrows the sky frequented by flocks of birds, Dhananjaya, O great king, became the destroyer of the Kurus.
Then with broad-headed arrows, razor-edged ones and spotless iron arrows Partha severed limbs and cut off heads.
The battlefield was covered with warriors with limbs cut off, without armour and without heads, fallen and falling all around.
With chariots, horses, men and elephants slain by Dhananjaya's arrows, the battlefield, O king, became like the great Vaitarani.
With broken poles, wheels and axles, horseless and horsed chariots of the fighters, with charioteers and with charioteers slain, the earth was strewn.
Armoured with golden mail, adorned with gold, the warriors on their mounts, angry rutting elephants of good breed, sent by enraged chief drivers, advanced against Arjuna.
Four hundred of them fell, slain by Kiritin with showers of arrows, like peaks of a great mountain overturned with their creatures.
With the ground strewn with the best elephants slain by Dhananjaya's arrows, Arjuna's chariot went on, as the sun piercing clouds.
The road was strewn by Phalguna with slain elephants, men and horses, with shattered chariots in many ways, with warriors lifeless without weapons, feathers and armour, with weapons cast aside.
He twanged Gandiva with a great terrible sound, a dreadful splitting like thunder in the sky.
Then the army was torn, struck by Dhananjaya's arrows, like a great ship in the sea tossed by a great wind.
Arrows of many forms, driven by Gandiva, like firebrands, meteors and thunderbolts, burned your army.
As a bamboo grove on a great mountain blazes at night, so your great army, pierced by arrows, quivered.
Crushed, burned, shattered, struck down by Kiritin with arrows, your army fled in all directions.
As herds of deer in a great forest are devoured by forest fire, so the Kurus turned about, burned by Savyasachin.
Then, leaving the mighty-armed Bhimasena in the battle, the whole Kuru army was agitated and turned away.
Then, when the Kurus were broken, the unconquered Bibhatsu met Bhimasena and stayed with him a moment.
Meeting Bhima and conferring with him, Phalguna told him that Yudhishthira was unharmed and free of pain.
With Bhimasena's leave, Dhananjaya then set out, making earth and sky resound with the roar of his chariot, O Bharata.
Then Dhananjaya was surrounded by ten dreadful chief foes, your sons, Duhshasana's younger brothers.
They tormented him with arrows like an elephant with firebrands; fierce, with bows strung, as if dancing, O Bharata.
Madhusudana made them circle to the left with his chariot; then the heroes fled, turned away from Arjuna's chariot.
Partha quickly felled their banners, chariots, bows and arrows with iron arrows and half-moon arrows.
Then with ten other broad-headed arrows he felled their heads; with eyes red with rage and lips bitten, those faces on the ground shone like clusters of stars in the sky.
Piercing those ten Kauravas, with golden armlets, with ten very swift broad-headed arrows with golden feathers, the destroyer of foes went on.
Krishna drove the white, very swift horses adorned with gold and covered with nets of pearls towards Karna's chariot.
As Dhananjaya went towards Karna's chariot, slaying foes, the Samshaptaka chariot-warriors followed, striking him with showers of arrows.
Arjuna with sharp arrows slew ninety of those hasting heroes with their charioteers, bows and banners.
They fell, slain by Kiritin's arrows of many forms, like siddhas with their celestial cars falling from heaven when their merit is exhausted.
Then the Kurus, best of the Kurus, with chariots, elephants and horses, fearless, advanced against the best of the Bharatas, Phalguna.
Dhananjaya held back that great army of your sons, exerted, with weapons unreleased and with its great elephants raised.
The mighty archers of the Kurus covered the delight of the Kurus with darts, spears, javelins, lances, maces, swords and arrows.
The Pandava dispelled that spread-out, raised shower of weapons of the Kurus with arrows as the sun darkness with rays.
Then, by your son's order, Mlecchas on thirteen hundred rutting elephants struck Partha on the flank.
With karnis, nalikas, iron arrows, javelins, spears, darts, kampanas and bhindipalas they tormented Partha on his chariot.
That shower of weapons loosed by the Yavanas on elephants, Phalguna, smiling, cut with sharp broad-headed and half-moon arrows.
Then he split all those elephants, with their pennants and riders, with great arrows of many marks, as the thunderbolt splits mountains.
Covered with golden-feathered arrows, the golden-garlanded great elephants fell slain like mountains with blazing flames.
Then a great roar of Gandiva arose, O lord of men, and the groaning and crying of men, elephants and horses.
Elephants slain, O king, fled on every side, and horses with riders slain ran in all ten directions.
Chariots bereft, O great king, of chariot-warriors and horses were seen by thousands like gandharva cities.
Horsemen, O great king, running here and there, were seen fallen there by Partha's arrows.
At that moment the strength of the Pandava's arms was seen, that alone he conquered horsemen, elephants and chariots in the battle.
Then Bhimasena, O king, seeing Kiritin surrounded by a great four-limbed force, O best of the Bharatas,
leaving the remnant of your slain chariots, rushed with speed, O king, to Dhananjaya's chariot.
Then that army, mostly slain and afflicted, fled; seeing Arjuna, Bhima went to his brother.
Bhima, unbewildered, mace in hand, destroyed in the great battle the surviving swift horses that Arjuna had left.
Like a most fierce night of destruction, devourer of men, elephants and horses, breaker of ramparts, towers and city gates, extremely terrible,
Bhima then quickly hurled his mace among men, elephants and horses; it killed many horses and horsemen, O revered one.
The Pandava crushed with his mace those men and horses in bronze and iron armour; they fell slain with a crash.
Having slain that elephant army, mighty Bhimasena mounted his own chariot again and followed Arjuna from behind.
That slain army, mostly turned away, dispirited, O great king, hung back, mostly caught in the toils of weapons.
Seeing that hanging, bold-less army stationed, Arjuna covered it with life-scorching arrows.
Then a cry of lament arose among the Kurus in the great battle as chariots, horses and elephants were being slain by Arjuna's arrows.
It stood crying "Alas," hiding behind one another; your army whirled like a firebrand wheel.
That army of yours, ablaze, its armour and bodies cut by arrows, was drenched in its own blood like a blooming ashoka forest.
Seeing Savyasachin's valour there, the Kurus all despaired of Karna's life.
Thinking Partha's fall of arrows in battle unbearable, the Kurus, conquered by the Gandiva-bowman, turned back.
Leaving Partha in the battle and slain by arrows, they fled in all directions in fear and cried out to the charioteer's son.
Partha pursued them, scattering many hundreds of arrows, gladdening the Pandava warriors led by Bhimasena.
Your sons, O great king, went to Karna's chariot on the road; to those sinking in the abyss, Karna was then the island.
The Kurus, O great king, like serpents deprived of poison, clung to Karna alone, from fear of the Gandiva-bowman.
As all beings frightened of death, O Bharata, cling to dharma, and as those with merit do,
so your sons, O lord of men, clung to the mighty-bowed Karna from terror of the great-souled Pandava.
To them, drenched with blood, fallen into bad plight, tormented by arrows, Karna said, "Do not be afraid; come to me from all sides."
Seeing his army broken by Partha by force, Karna stood stretching his bow, wishing to slay his foe; he ran again at the Panchalas in Savyasachin's sight.
Then in a moment the kings, their eyes red as blood, rained masses of arrows on Karna as clouds on a mountain.
Then thousands of arrows loosed by Karna, O revered one, separated the Panchalas from their lives, best of the living.
Then there was a great battle of the Panchalas, O lord of men, as they were slain by the charioteer's son, slayers of foes for their friends' sake.
Felling the charioteer from his chariot with an anjalika arrow, he killed Janamejaya's horses; he covered Shatanika and Sutasoma with broad-headed arrows and cut their bows.
He pierced Dhrishtadyumna with six, killed his right horse in battle, and having killed Satyaki's horses, the charioteer's son slew the Kaikeya's son, Vishoka.
When the prince was slain, the Kaikeya commander of fierce bow rushed at him and struck Karna's son Sushena, much pierced with swift fierce arrows.
Karna by force cut his arms and head with three half-moon arrows; he fell lifeless from the chariot to the ground, like a sala tree felled by axes.
Sushena, having covered the hero of the Shinis, his horses slain, with sharp swift arrows, dancing as it were, the charioteer's son, struck by Shaineya's arrows, fell.
With his son slain, Karna, his mind seized by rage, wishing to kill the bull of the Shinis, said "Shaineya, you are slain!" and loosed an arrow that foes could not bear.
Shikhandin cut that arrow and struck Karna with three each time; Karna cut his bow and banner and with two arrows killed Sujata.
The fierce, self-controlled one pierced Shikhandin with six and struck off Dhrishtadyumna's head; then the great-souled Adhiratha's son pierced Sutasoma with a sharp arrow.
Then the hero among men quickly smiled and drove his chariot to Adhiratha's son's chariot, wishing to protect them in fear, Subahu, struck by the leader of chariots.
Stretching Gandiva with its fierce roar and striking the string hard with his palm, suddenly making a darkness of arrows, he killed elephants, horses, chariots and men.
Bhimasena followed him in his chariot, guarding the Pandava, the sole hero, from behind; those two princes, swiftly in their chariots, freed from their foes, went to Karna.
In the meantime the charioteer's son made a great battle, crushing the Somakas; he killed throngs of chariots, horses and elephants and covered the quarters with arrows.
Uttamaujas and Janamejaya, the enraged Yudhamanyu and Shikhandin together roared at Karna with arrows, pressing him together with the Parshata.
Those five Panchala chariot-warriors, attacking Karna Vaikartana with fair arrows, could not dislodge him from his chariot, as senses cannot dislodge a self-controlled man by fortitude.
Cutting their bows, banners, horses, charioteers, quivers and pennants with arrows, he struck those five with arrows and Karna roared like a lion.
As he shot and slew them, with the sound of the bow and bowstring, the people sank, thinking the earth with its mountains and trees was splitting.
With the bow like Shakra's, drawn full, Adhiratha's son loosing arrows shone in the battle, with a circle of blazing rays, like the sun in the rains.
He pierced Shikhandin with twelve sharp arrows, then Uttamaujas with six, Yudhamanyu with swift three, and the Somaka and Parshata's son with three each.

Those five great chariot-warriors were defeated in the great battle, O revered one, by the charioteer's son, and stood without exertion, tamers of foes, like senses conquered by one master of objects.
As merchants with a wrecked ship are lifted from the sea by boats, so the sons of Draupadi lifted their maternal uncles out of the sea of Karna with well-prepared chariots.
Then the bull of the Shinis, cutting the arrows sent by Karna with sharp arrows, split Karna with sharp iron arrows and pierced your eldest son with eight.
Kripa, Bhoja, your son and Karna himself struck him with sharp arrows; the best of the Yadus fought those four like the lord of the daityas with the lords of the quarters.
With the bow of equal tension, roaring, drawn hard, rain of immeasurable arrows, Satyaki became very hard to withstand, shining like the sun in mid-sky.
Again the tamers of foes, well armoured, in chariots protected the hero of the Shinis; the Panchala chariots meeting in the great battle were like the Maruts with Shakra in subduing foes.
Then a most dreadful battle took place between your foes and your soldiers, with destruction of chariots, horses and elephants, as of old between the gods and the asuras.
Chariots, elephants, horses and foot-soldiers wandered, rained on by weapons of many kinds, stumbling, struck by each other, roaring in distress and falling lifeless.
Seeing the situation, your son, the king's younger brother, ran, scattering arrows, at Bhima; Vrikodara rushed at him swiftly, as a lion on a great deer.
Then a superhuman battle took place between those two, a gamble with their lives for stake, of the two raging and fierce ones, like Shambara and Shakra.
With keen, body-ending arrows they struck each other hard, like two great elephants, once rutting, in a time of desire, their minds set on a female.
Then Vrikodara, in haste, cut your son's bow and banner with two razor-arrows, split his forehead with a feathered arrow and struck off his charioteer's head from his body.
That prince, taking another bow, pierced Vrikodara with twelve, himself controlling the horses, and rained straight arrows on Bhima again.
Then the high-souled one quickly pierced Bhimasena with many excellent arrows; he, streaming like an elephant in rut, hurled a mace at him in the tumult.
With it Bhimasena took Duhshasana by force over ten bow-lengths; struck by that swift mace, Duhshasana fell trembling.
His horses and charioteer were slain, O king, and his chariot crushed as it fell; his armour, ornaments, garments and garland shattered, writhing, tormented by great pain.
Then the mighty Bhimasena, remembering the hostility your sons had practised, leapt from his chariot to the ground and, with effort, fixed his eyes on him.

Drawing a sharp sword with a good edge, stepping on the throat of the trembling one, he tore open the breast of the fallen man on the ground and drank his warm blood; tasting it again and again, looking at him, enraged, he spoke exceedingly.

Of mother's milk, of honey and ghee, of fermented honey-drink well made, of divine water, of milk and curd, or the best of churned butter—this taste, I deem, of the enemy's blood is better than all of these today.
Even those who saw Bhimasena then, speaking thus, running again and leaping, greatly delighted, fell down pained in fear.
And those men who fell there, from whose hands weapons fell, cried out loudly in fear; with eyes shut, they did not see it.
All who saw Bhima there on every side, drinking Duhshasana's blood, fled in terror, saying, "This is not a man."
In the hearing of the world's heroes he said this: "I drink your blood from your throat, lowest of men; say now, enraged, again 'Cow! Cow!'
Sleeping on the edge of the pramana tree, the Kalakuta poison for food, bites of serpents, hardship, and burning in the house of lac,
the seizing of the kingdom by dice, living in the forest, the unhappiness in battles with bows and arrows and in the house—
these sorrows we know, never joys, because of the wickedness of Dhritarashtra and his sons, always."
Having said these words, O king, victorious, Vrikodara said again, O great king, to the two Krishnas, who smiled:

What I promised regarding Duhshasana in battle, all that has been done here today, heroes. Today I shall give another, a second: Duryodhana, as a sacrificial beast, having killed him, and crushing the head of the evil-souled one with my foot in the sight of the Kauravas I shall find peace.
Having said so much, delighted, with limbs drenched in blood, he roared aloud, and the very strong great soul danced as Sahasranetra (Indra) having slain Vritra.
Kavachin, Nishangin, Pashin, Dandadhara, Dhanurdhara, Alolupa, Shala, Sandha, and Vatavega and Suvarchas,
these, gathered together, afflicted by the calamity of their brother, held back the mighty-armed Bhimasena with arrows.
Held back on every side by those great chariot-warriors with arrows, Bhima, his eyes red with rage, shone enraged like Death.
Those, with ten swift broad-headed arrows each, golden-armleted and golden-feathered, Partha (Bhima) sent to Yama's abode.
When those heroes were slain, your army fled in the sight of the charioteer's son, afflicted by fear of the Pandava.
Then Karna, O great king, entered the great battle, seeing Bhima's prowess like Death among creatures.
Shalya, ornament of the battle, knowing his appearance and feelings, said to Karna the word suited to the time, tamer of foes: "Do not be distressed, Radheya; this does not become you.
These kings flee, afflicted by fear of Bhimasena, and Duryodhana is dazed, grieved by the calamity of his brother.
With Duhshasana's blood being drunk by the great soul, they are dull in mind and their rage is struck by grief.
Kripa and the others and the brothers surviving Karna's slaying wait on Duryodhana, surrounding him on every side.
The Pandavas have attained their aim, led by Dhananjaya, and the brave stand ready to fight facing you.
So, tiger among men, standing in great manliness, putting forward the duty of a kshatriya, go against Dhananjaya.
The whole burden has been laid on you by Dhritarashtra's son; bear it, mighty-armed one, as best you can; in victory there will be great fame, in defeat sure heaven.
And Vrishasena, Radheya, your son, enraged, runs at the Pandavas while you are bewildered."
Hearing these words of Shalya of immeasurable splendour, he made his human nature in his heart firm for battle.
Then the enraged Vrishasena ran at Vrikodara, who stood on his own chariot, having slain foes, like Death with a raised rod, mace in hand, crushing your men.
Nakula, the hero, ran at him in rage, tormenting his foe with arrows, at Karna's son delighted in the battle, as Jishnu, Maghavan, wishing to kill Jambha.
Then the hero Nakula with a razor-arrow cut his banner, variegated with crystal conch, and the variegated bow of Karna's son with a broad-headed arrow bound with gold.
Then Karna's son, taking another bow quickly, pierced the Pandava with divine great weapons, skilled in great weapons, wishing to take revenge for Duhshasana.
Then the high-souled Nakula, enraged, pierced him with arrows like great meteors; and Karna's son, skilled in weapons, pierced Nakula with divine weapons.
Karna's son, O king, destroyed all Nakula's horses with the best weapons—Vanayu horses, white, gold-adorned, swift, of the delicate prince.
Then, descending from the chariot whose horses were slain, taking a fair shield with eight moons and a sword like the sky, leaping, he ranged like a bird.
Then, ranging in many paths in the air, he cut men, horses and elephants; they fell cut by the sword to the ground, like animals at a horse sacrifice for the slaughterer.
Two thousand known battle-brave men of many countries, well-fed and true to their word, were quickly cut down by Nakula alone, like fine sandalwood for its essence.
Karna's son, attacking him as he came on, pierced Nakula on all sides with arrows; Nakula, tormented by arrows, pierced the hero, who in turn grew angry.
As he, alone, destroyed men, horses, elephants and chiefs of chariots, as in sport, the son of Karna pierced the hero with eighteen arrows, and he grew angry.
Then the Pandava hero, wishing to kill Karna's son, rushed at him in battle; Karna's son destroyed his thousand-starred shield with his arrows in the great battle.
His iron sword, sharp-edged, capable of bearing great weight, taker of foes' bodies, most dreadful, like a fierce serpent brandished—
the tamer of foes quickly cut that sword with six keen dreadful arrows, and again struck him hard in the chest with sharp drunk arrows.
And with other friends, kinsmen and well-wishers, he brooded on that very matter, Karna's death.
Then, when the sun reached the best of mountains, setting, night came, nurse of the whole world.
Your minister Duhshasana and the evil-souled Radheya, the wicked Shakuni, the ill-minded Chitrasena and Shalya—by whom the whole world was made a thorn.
I, not knowing, was in the battle eager for the kingdom and had him slain; that burns my limbs like fire a heap of cotton.

[Gautami said:] "What gain is there in seizing and killing an enemy? What peace is there after getting an enemy and saying 'Hail'? Why, gentle one, should I not forgive the serpent, or what reason is there not to do his release?"
Such as you, of great intellect, this does not become today; what is to be known you know, and what is to be done you have done.
Hearing the sensible words of the king of dharma, they then behaved especially well, except Bhima alone.
They reported to the king the dreadful offspring of the curse; the king, dejected, had it ground to fine powder.
Kripa and the others surrounded Yuyutsu; Ulupi, the Naga's daughter, entered the Ganga, O Kaurava.
Where are those kings, Brahmana? I see them, Narada: Virata and Drupada and those led by Dhrishtaketu—
